newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi army denies reported slaughter of 400.
newsitem.headline: Burundi army denies reported slaughter of 400.

text.p: Eyewitnesses said on Friday Burundi troops led the slaughter of 400 civilians in the northwestern province of Muramvya early this month but the army denied the report.
The witnesses, who declined to be identified, said the 400 were killed in Bukeye commune in Muramvya province on January 5 by troops armed with guns and displaced Tutsis with machetes and clubs.
A spokesman for the Tutsi-dominated army, which earlier this month admitted killing 126 Hutu refugees who had returned from Zaire, denied the report as "absolutely and completely false".
"Nothing happened in Bukeye on January 5," said army spokesman Lieutenant-Colonel Isaie Nibizi in Bujumbura.
The witnesses said troops and displaced Tutsis set out from Kayanza's Rango commune bordering on Bukeye and from Mbuye in Muramvya on January 5 and drove the civilian population into valleys.

"They attacked around 7.30 in the morning, the soldiers using guns and dislodging the panic-stricken fugitives, the displaced people killing with machetes and cudgels," a wounded witness told Studio Ijambo, an independent radio production unit.
A total of 304 people were killed at Gatara valley between Bukeye and Rango -- many of them women, children and old people unable to flee fast enough to escape, the eyewitnesses said.
Another 100 attempting to hide between Nyabiture and Gitangaro were also killed with bayonets and clubs, they added.
"Some of the bodies are still there, their intestines trailing in the Muzi stream," a witness said. It was impossible to obtain independent comment on the reported killings.
More than 150,000 people have been killed in war between the army and Hutu rebels and massacres since October 1993 when Burundi's first elected Hutu president was murdered in an attempted coup.
Human rights groups accuse both the army and Hutu rebels of killing civilians in reprisal attacks. The army said last week it had killed 126 Hutu refugees forced back home by Tanzanian authorities.

Burundi's military leader Pierre Buyoya, who seized power in an army coup from the Hutu civilian president in July, met Rwanda's President Pasteur Bizimungu in southern Rwanda on Thursday, a spokesman said.
"The talked about the situation in Burundi and the situation in the Great Lakes region," said Buyoya's spokesman Jean-Luc Ndizeye of the their meeting in the southern city of Butare.
It was their first meeting since Buyoya seized power.
Relations between Rwanda and Burundi were strained by reports of indiscriminate army killings in the wake of the coup, senior Rwandan officials say. Buyoya said he took power to bring peace.
Regional states including Rwanda clamped an economic and transport blockade on Burundi one week after the coup in an attempt to force Buyoya into peace negotiations with rebels of the Hutu majority.
Buyoya's government is due to start preparatory meetings on January 27 for a "National Debate" as part of its three-year transitional programme. The rebels will be excluded from the talks.
